abstract: NBER Working Paper 35275 (May 2026, revised September 2026) by Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang studies three generations of AI coding tools (autocomplete, sync agents such as locally run Claude Code, async agents such as cloud Codex) using more than 500,000 GitHub developers and Microsoft telemetry, 2022-2026. In a matched event study, the tools raise weekly commits cumulatively by about 30%, 180% and 240%. Gains attenuate sharply up the production chain: the 240% effect on commits falls to 80% for projects and 30% for releases. Sync agents raise lines of code 958% and pull requests 86% but releases only 20%. Most attenuation reflects experimentation rather than larger releases: after sync-agent adoption developers add 7.0 times as many lines but delete 12.2 times as many, create 79% more branches, and the share of new repositories abandoned after a month rose from 60% to 69% since 2021. A hierarchical CES model implies an elasticity of substitution of 0.23 between AI-assisted output and human effort, meaning strong complementarity and weak-link bottlenecks. In four app marketplaces new-app entry roughly doubled from early 2025 but total usage did not rise.
keyFindings: Autocomplete, sync agents and async agents raise commits cumulatively by about 30%, 180% and 240%.
The 240% cumulative commit effect falls to 80% for projects and 30% for releases.
Sync agents raise lines of code by 958% and pull requests by 86%, but releases by only 20%; autocomplete: 234% lines, 30% commits, 9% releases.
Estimated elasticity of substitution between AI and human effort of 0.23, indicating strong complementarity.
Monthly new-app entry roughly doubled across the Apple App Store, Google Play, Chrome Web Store and SourceForge since early 2025, with no increase in total usage.
The share of new repositories with no activity after their first month rose 9 percentage points since 2021, from 60% to 69%.
methodology: Matched event study: each adopting developer is matched to a similarly active control in the same calendar week one year earlier, to avoid contamination from contemporaneous private AI use, matched on 11 weeks of pre-treatment activity. Adoption is dated from public GitHub signals and internal Microsoft telemetry across GitHub Copilot, Claude and Codex. Outcomes span lines, files, commits, PRs, repositories and releases. Placebo tests on non-AI tools; hierarchical CES model calibrated to the attenuation pattern; monthly app-marketplace panels. Open-source software.
qualifiers: Tier 1 by repo convention for NBER working papers; not peer-reviewed. Observational, not randomised: adoption is self-selected, mitigated by matching, placebo and pre-trend tests. Open-source developers and public app stores may not represent proprietary enterprise software. One or more co-authors disclosed relevant relationships (Microsoft data). The paper measures productivity and output, not employment; it does not estimate labor-demand effects. Commit gains are not time savings per task and should not be compared with RCT time-saved estimates.
